chapters.title: Taking lunch apart, molecule by molecule

lines.cap: Right now, coiled up inside you, is a tube about as long as two cars parked end to end.
In there, your lunch is being taken apart, molecule by molecule, surrounded by acid strong enough to dissolve metal. So why doesn't your stomach digest itself?
This is **digestion**: breaking food down into molecules small enough to get into your blood.
Let's build a balanced diet, test some foods, then follow a sandwich all the way through you.

chapters.title: A balanced diet: seven nutrient groups

lines.cap: A **balanced diet** contains all the nutrients your body needs, in the **right amounts**. Scientists sort them into **seven groups**.
Remember them with **C**razy **P**eople **F**ind **V**ery **M**any **F**ish **W**et: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water.
**Carbohydrates** are your **main source of energy**. You get them from bread, rice, pasta, potatoes and sugar.
**Proteins** are for **growth and repair** of cells and tissues. Think meat, fish, eggs, beans and nuts.
**Fats**, or **lipids**, are a **store of energy**. They also **insulate** you and **protect** your organs. They're in butter, oils, cheese and nuts.
So fat isn't bad in itself. Problems come from eating far **more energy** than you use.
**Vitamins** are needed in **tiny amounts** to keep your body working, like **vitamin C** from fruit and vegetables.
**Minerals** are needed in tiny amounts too, like **iron** from red meat for red blood cells, and **calcium** from milk for bones and teeth.
**Fibre**, from wholegrains, fruit and vegetables, can't be digested. But it isn't useless: it adds **bulk**, so your gut can push food along.
And **water**, about two-thirds of your body, is the **solvent** that reactions happen in, and it carries substances around.
Fibre and water give no energy, but they're **essential**. And no single food has everything, so **variety** matters.
Food labels list these same nutrients, to help you compare foods.
If a nutrient is missing from your diet for a long time, you can develop a **deficiency disease**.
It's caused by a **lack** of something, not by a germ, so you can't catch it.
Too little **vitamin C** causes **scurvy**: bleeding gums, and wounds that heal slowly. Vitamin C is needed to make healthy connective tissue.
A naval doctor, James Lind, showed in 1747 that oranges and lemons could cure sailors of scurvy: one of the first clinical trials.
Too little **vitamin D** or **calcium** causes **rickets**: children's bones become soft, weak and bent.
Vitamin D helps your gut **absorb calcium**. You get it from oily fish and eggs, and your skin makes it in **sunlight**.
Too little **iron** causes **anaemia**: too few red blood cells, so less oxygen is carried, and you feel **tired** and look **pale**.
And too little **fibre** causes **constipation**: without bulk, your gut muscles struggle to push waste along.
**Energy needs** vary too. They depend on your **age**, how **active** you are, your **body size** and **sex**, and on **pregnancy**.
Growing teenagers need lots of energy for their size, and an athlete needs far more than an office worker.
Take in much more energy than you use, and you **gain weight**; much less, and you lose weight and feel tired. **Balance** is the goal.
How can you tell which nutrients a food contains? With chemical tests that each give a **colour change**.
For **starch**, add orange-brown **iodine** solution. If starch is there, it turns **blue-black**.
Don't get it backwards: iodine **starts** orange-brown. With no starch, it stays orange-brown.
For **reducing sugars**, like glucose, add blue **Benedict's solution**, then **heat** it in a water bath.
If sugar is there, it changes from blue, to green, to yellow, to orange, and finally to **brick-red**.
The heating is essential: no heat, no colour change.
For **protein**, add **biuret** solution. It turns from blue to **purple**, or lilac.
For **fat**, do the **ethanol emulsion test**: shake the food with ethanol, then pour it into water. Fat makes a **cloudy white emulsion**.
The stronger the colour, the **more** of that nutrient there is.
And always run a **control**: a tube with water and no food, so you know what a negative result looks like.
Most of the food you eat is made of **large, insoluble molecules**: long chains, like starch and protein.
They're far **too big** to pass through the wall of your gut into your blood.
**Digestion** breaks these large, insoluble molecules down into **small, soluble** ones.
Now they can be **absorbed** into your blood, and carried to every cell, for energy, growth and repair.
**Starch** is broken down into **glucose**.
**Protein** is broken down into **amino acids**.
And **fat** is broken down into **fatty acids and glycerol**.
Two kinds of digestion work together. **Mechanical** digestion physically breaks food into smaller pieces, like your teeth chewing, or your stomach churning.
**Chemical** digestion uses **enzymes** to break the bonds inside the molecules.
Smaller pieces have a much bigger **surface area**, so the enzymes have more to work on.
Try it at home: squish torn-up bread and water in a sealed bag for two minutes, like stomach muscles. It turns to soupy mush.

chapters.title: The alimentary canal: mouth to anus

lines.cap: Food travels through one long, muscular tube, from your mouth to your anus: the **alimentary canal**.
In the **mouth**, your teeth chew the food, and **saliva** adds an enzyme called **amylase**, and makes it slippery to swallow.
The **oesophagus** carries it down to your stomach.
The **stomach** is a muscular bag. It churns the food, and adds **acid** and an enzyme called **protease**.
So why doesn't it digest itself? Its wall is coated in a thick layer of slimy **mucus**, and it replaces its lining cells every few days.
In the **small intestine**, digestion is **finished**, and the small molecules are **absorbed** into your blood.
So digestion is **not** just a stomach job: it **starts** in your mouth, and **finishes** in your small intestine.
The **large intestine** absorbs **water** from what's left.
The **rectum** stores the solid waste, called **faeces**, until it leaves through the **anus**.
To remember the order: **M**y **O**ld **S**tomach **S**ometimes **L**oves **R**oast **A**nchovies. Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum, anus.
Three organs help, but food never passes through them. The **liver** makes **bile**, the **gall bladder** stores it, and the **pancreas** makes digestive enzymes.
So they're **not** part of the alimentary canal. Don't list them in it!

chapters.title: Enzymes and bile: the chemical workers

lines.cap: Chemical digestion is done by **enzymes**: **biological catalysts** that **speed up** reactions without being used up.
Enzymes aren't alive. They're molecules made by your cells, and one enzyme can work on molecule after molecule.
First, **amylase** breaks down **starch** into **sugars**. It's made in your **salivary glands** and **pancreas**.
**Protease** breaks down **protein** into **amino acids**. It's made in your **stomach** and **pancreas**.
**Lipase** breaks down **fats** into **fatty acids and glycerol**. It's made in your **pancreas**.
The names help: **p**rotease for **p**rotein, **l**ipase for **l**ipids, and **a**mylase for st**a**rch.
Each enzyme is **specific**: it only fits one kind of molecule, like a key that fits just one lock.
That's why people with **lactose intolerance** struggle with milk: they don't make enough of the one enzyme that digests milk sugar.
Enzymes need the right conditions too: stomach protease works best in **acid**, but small-intestine enzymes prefer slightly **alkaline**.
Then there's **bile**, made by the **liver** and stored in the **gall bladder**. Bile is **not** an enzyme, but it has two big jobs.
First, it **emulsifies** fat, breaking big blobs into lots of tiny droplets. That's a much bigger **surface area**, so lipase works faster.
Second, bile is **alkaline**, so it **neutralises** the stomach acid, giving the small intestine's enzymes the conditions they need.
**Biological washing powders** use protease and lipase too, to digest blood and grease stains, even in a cool wash.
Once food is digested, the small molecules are **absorbed** from the gut into the blood, mainly in the **small intestine**.
Its inner wall is covered in millions of tiny, finger-like bumps called **villi**. Just one is called a **villus**.
Zoom in on one villus, and you'll find four adaptations.
One: a **large surface area**. Spread flat, the lining of your small intestine would cover about **30 m²**: roughly half a badminton court.
Two: a **thin wall**, just **one cell thick**, so molecules only have a **short distance** to travel.
Three: a **good blood supply**. **Capillaries** carry away the glucose and amino acids, keeping the concentration gradient steep.
Four: a **lacteal** in the middle, which absorbs the products of **fat** digestion.
Remember: **B**ig, **T**hin, **B**loody **L**acteal. Big surface area, thin wall, blood supply, and a lacteal.
What's left moves on to the **large intestine**, which absorbs most of the **remaining water**, leaving solid faeces.
Trillions of bacteria live there too, feeding on fibre you can't digest. Scientists are only beginning to learn how they affect your health.
And what moves food along? **Peristalsis**: waves of muscle contraction that squeeze behind the food and push it forward, like toothpaste in a tube.
It doesn't rely on gravity, so you could even swallow a meal hanging upside down!
And the stomach's **hydrochloric acid** doesn't digest food itself. It **kills harmful microbes**, and gives protease the **acidic** conditions it needs.
Now back to where digestion **begins**: your mouth, where your **teeth** carry out **mechanical digestion**.
Chewing doesn't change food **chemically**. It just cuts and crushes it into smaller pieces, with a **larger surface area** for enzymes.
You have **four types** of teeth, each shaped for a different job.
At the front are the **incisors**: flat, chisel-shaped teeth that **cut** and **bite** off pieces of food.
**Canines** are the pointed teeth just behind them. They **grip** and **tear** food, especially meat.
**Premolars** are broad teeth with bumpy tops. They **crush** and **grind**.
**Molars** are the big teeth at the back. They **grind** and chew food into a soft pulp.
Your tongue moves the food around, and saliva turns it into a soft ball, called a **bolus**, that's easy to swallow.
Try this: hold a plain cracker on your tongue for a minute, without chewing. Slowly, it starts to taste **sweet**.
That's the **amylase** in your saliva, breaking starch into sugar: proof that **chemical** digestion starts in your mouth too.
So look after your teeth: brush them twice a day, and cut down on sugary food and drinks.

chapters.title: Egestion and excretion: not the same

lines.cap: Two words both mean getting rid of waste, but in science they're **different**: **egestion** and **excretion**.
**Egestion** is removing **undigested food**. Fibre, dead gut cells and other leftovers form **faeces**, which leave through the **anus**.
Faeces were **never absorbed**. They never entered your cells or your blood, so egestion is **not** excretion.
**Excretion** removes the waste made by your body's **own chemical reactions**, inside your cells.
**Carbon dioxide** is a waste product of **respiration**. Your **lungs** excrete it when you breathe out.
**Urea** is made by your **liver** from extra amino acids. Your **kidneys** remove it, in **urine**.
Extra water and salts leave in urine and sweat, too.
So ask: did the waste come from food that was **never used**? That's called egestion. From your body's **own reactions**? That's excretion.

chapters.title: Recap: memory hooks and exam traps

lines.cap: Let's lock it all in.
**Crazy People Find Very Many Fish Wet**: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water.
**My Old Stomach Sometimes Loves Roast Anchovies**: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum, anus.
**Protease** for protein, **lipase** for lipids, **amylase** for starch.
**Big, Thin, Bloody Lacteal**: the four adaptations of a villus.
Now, five exam traps to avoid.
One: Benedict's solution must be **heated**. No heat, no result.
Two: iodine starts **orange-brown** and turns **blue-black** with starch, not the other way round.
Three: bile **emulsifies** fat. It doesn't digest it: it's **lipase** that does.
Four: the liver, gall bladder and pancreas are **not** part of the alimentary canal.
Five: fat gives fatty acids **and** glycerol, and protein gives **amino acids**.
Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
Which food test must be heated, and what colour shows a positive result?
**Benedict's** test, for reducing sugar. It turns **brick-red**.
Which enzyme digests fat, and what does it make?
It's **lipase**, making **fatty acids and glycerol**.
A lack of which vitamin causes scurvy?
**Vitamin C.**
Name two ways a villus is adapted for absorption.
Any two of: a **large surface area**, a **thin wall**, a **good blood supply**, and a **lacteal**.
True or false: getting rid of faeces is called excretion.
**False.** That's called **egestion**. Faeces were never absorbed into your body.
Brilliant work. Now try the Food & Digestion quiz in your Science Lab, to lock it in.
